title: Enthalpy changes and energy cycles
summary: Reactions transfer energy to or from the surroundings. Measure enthalpy changes by calorimetry, use bond enthalpies and Hess's law; at HL, use formation and combustion data and Born–Haber cycles.

keyterms.definition: A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative and the surroundings warm up.
A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive and the surroundings cool.
The heat transferred at constant pressure, in kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
Pressure 100 kPa, solution concentrations 1 mol dm⁻³, usually quoted at 298 K; shown by the ⦵ symbol.
Measuring temperature change to find heat transferred: Q = mcΔT, then ΔH = −Q/n.
Energy needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 K; for water 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Energy needed to break one mole of a given bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over many compounds.
The total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided start and end states are the same.
Diagram of potential energy along the reaction pathway showing reactants, products, activation energy and ΔH.
Enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states; zero for elements.
Enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
An energy cycle applying Hess's law to the formation of an ionic compound, used to find lattice enthalpy.

options: ΔH is negative and the surroundings warm
products have more enthalpy than reactants
ΔH is positive and the surroundings cool
questions.explanation: Energy is released to the surroundings, so products are lower in enthalpy.

questions.statement: Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water makes the water colder, so the process is endothermic.
questions.explanation: Heat is absorbed from the water (surroundings), lowering its temperature; ΔH > 0.

questions.text: Heating 50.0 g of water by 10.0 K requires ___ J (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).

questions.prompt: 0.0500 mol of acid is neutralized and releases 2.85 kJ. What is ΔH?
questions.explanation: ΔH = −Q/n = −2.85 / 0.0500 = −57.0 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because heat is released).

questions.prompt: Match each feature of an energy profile.

pairs.right: Reactants up to the transition state

questions.explanation: Ea is always positive; ΔH can be negative or positive.

questions.statement: The experimental ΔH from a simple coffee-cup calorimeter is usually less exothermic than the literature value.
questions.explanation: Heat loss to the surroundings means the measured temperature rise is too small.

questions.prompt: Which is the main source of systematic error in a simple calorimetry experiment?
questions.explanation: Heat lost to air and the container makes ΔT too small; insulation and extrapolating a cooling curve help.

questions.text: Standard conditions use a pressure of ___ kPa.
questions.explanation: The IB uses 100 kPa as standard pressure.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a solution calorimetry experiment.
items: Measure a known volume of solution into an insulated cup
Record the initial temperature for a few minutes
Add the second reactant and stir
Record the temperature until it peaks and starts to fall
Extrapolate the cooling line to find ΔT
questions.explanation: Extrapolation corrects for heat lost while the reaction proceeds.

questions.prompt: In Q = mcΔT for a solution reaction, m is usually taken as…
options: the mass of the solid reactant
the mass of the solution (≈ volume of water in cm³ × 1 g cm⁻³)
questions.explanation: The water absorbs or supplies the heat; its density is taken as 1.00 g cm⁻³.
Energy must be supplied to separate bonded atoms; forming bonds releases energy.
Bond breaking is endothermic (positive); bond forming is exothermic (subtracted).

questions.prompt: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond enthalpies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH is…

questions.statement: Values calculated from average bond enthalpies are approximate.
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpies are averages across many compounds and apply to gases only.

questions.prompt: By Hess's law, if A → B has ΔH = −100 kJ and B → C has ΔH = +40 kJ, then A → C has ΔH =
questions.explanation: Add the steps: −100 + 40 = −60 kJ.

questions.text: If a reaction is reversed, the sign of ΔH is ___.
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction has the same magnitude but opposite sign.

questions.prompt: Match each change to the enthalpy adjustment.
questions.explanation: Manipulate equations to build the target, applying the same changes to ΔH.

questions.statement: A strong bond has a low bond enthalpy.
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpy measures the energy needed to break the bond, so stronger bonds have higher values.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a Hess's law calculation using given equations.
items: Identify where each target species appears in the given equations
Reverse or multiply given equations as needed
Add the manipulated equations and cancel species
questions.explanation: The manipulated equations must sum to the target equation.

questions.prompt: Why is the ΔH of combustion of methane calculated from bond enthalpies different from the data-booklet value?
options: Water is a liquid under standard conditions, but bond enthalpies apply to gases
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpies are averages for gaseous species; condensing water releases extra energy.

questions.prompt: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of O₂(g)?
questions.explanation: Elements in their standard states have ΔHf⦵ = 0 by definition.
Products minus reactants, multiplied by their coefficients.

questions.prompt: Use ΔHf⦵: CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286, CH₄(g) −75 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔHc⦵ of CH₄ is…

questions.explanation: With combustion data the cycle runs through combustion products, so it is reactants minus products.

questions.prompt: Match each Born–Haber step to its sign.
questions.explanation: The large exothermic lattice formation makes the overall ΔHf negative.

questions.prompt: Order the Born–Haber steps for forming NaCl(s) from its elements.
items: Cl(g) gains an electron to form Cl⁻(g)
questions.explanation: One common order; the cycle total equals ΔHf of NaCl.

questions.prompt: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation of water?
questions.explanation: One mole of product from elements in their standard states.

questions.text: In a Born–Haber cycle, lattice enthalpy is found using ___ law.
questions.explanation: It cannot be measured directly, so it is calculated from the other steps.

questions.statement: The second electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic.
questions.explanation: Adding an electron to O⁻ requires work against repulsion, so it is endothermic.

questions.prompt: ΔHf⦵ values: NH₃(g) −46, NO(g) +90, H₂O(g) −242 kJ mol⁻¹. For 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, ΔH⦵ is…
